claims.text: In high-entropy alloys composed of early and late transition metals, superconducting Tc is primarily governed by average valence electron count.
Changing average valence electron count shifts the Fermi level and changes the density of states at the Fermi level.
The density of states at the Fermi level controls the electron-phonon coupling strength.
Changes in electron-phonon coupling produce systematic shifts in Tc in accordance with BCS theory.
A Ti-V-Cr-Zr-Mo alloy can be produced by arc melting and homogenization as a homogeneous, single-phase disordered solid solution.
The proposed starting alloy contains at least five elements and is within the high-entropy-alloy regime.
Replacing Cr with Mn or Fe can systematically vary average valence electron count while retaining the original level of chemical disorder.
XRD and TEM can be used to assess whether the substituted alloys remain single-phase and disordered.
Arc melting followed by homogenization near 1000 degrees Celsius for 24 hours is an applicable synthesis schedule for the proposed alloy series.
The proposed initial Ti-V-Cr-Zr-Mo alloy has a measurable baseline superconducting transition temperature above the approximately 1.8 K measurement floor.
Increasing average valence electron count relative to the baseline will increase Tc.
Decreasing average valence electron count relative to the baseline will decrease Tc.
Tc will vary monotonically with average valence electron count across the substitution series.
The proposed valence-electron-count relationship applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase disordered solid solution.
Phase segregation, significant local ordering, or emergent magnetic impurities can invalidate the proposed relationship.
Local ordering and defects may independently influence superconducting behavior in the proposed alloys.
Multiband effects may occur in the proposed high-entropy alloys.
Electronic specific heat can be used to estimate the density of states at the Fermi level.
The absence of a systematic Tc-versus-valence-electron-count trend in a phase-preserved substitution series would falsify the hypothesis.
The occurrence of phase segregation or significant local ordering during substitution would itself falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary field excludes phase-segregated or significantly ordered samples from the hypothesis's domain, whereas the falsification rule says that observing those out-of-domain states would falsify the hypothesis. Such observations should instead invalidate the comparison unless a phase-preserved trend is also tested.
